code: install.packages("arules") library(arules)

title: Getting started with arules
text: named list simplest input format small data sets. summary() describes sparse transaction matrix. itemFrequency() returns fraction transactions containing item.
code: baskets <- list(   T1 = c("milk", "bread", "butter"),   T2 = c("bread", "butter"),   T3 = c("milk", "bread"),   T4 = c("bread", "jam"),   T5 = c("milk", "bread", "butter"),   T6 = c("beer", "chips"),   T7 = c("beer", "chips", "salsa"),   T8 = c("bread", "butter", "jam") ) trans <- transactions(baskets) trans #> transactions in sparse format with #>  8 transactions (rows) and #>  7 items (columns) inspect(trans[1:3]) #>     items                 transactionID #> [1] {bread, butter, milk} T1            #> [2] {bread, butter}       T2            #> [3] {bread, milk}         T3 summary(trans) #> transactions as itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  8 rows (elements/itemsets/transactions) and #>  7 columns (items) and a density of 0.3571429  #>  #> most frequent items: #>   bread  butter    milk    beer   chips (Other)  #>       6       4       3       2       2       3  #>  #> element (itemset/transaction) length distribution: #> sizes #> 2 3  #> 4 4  #>  #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  #>     2.0     2.0     2.5     2.5     3.0     3.0  #>  #> includes extended item information - examples: #>   labels #> 1   beer #> 2  bread #> 3 butter #>  #> includes extended transaction information - examples: #>   transactionID #> 1            T1 #> 2            T2 #> 3            T3 sort(itemFrequency(trans), decreasing = TRUE) #>  bread butter   milk   beer  chips    jam  salsa  #>  0.750  0.500  0.375  0.250  0.250  0.250  0.125

title: Getting started with arules
text: apriori() mines association rules. Support specifies often items rule must occur together, confidence specifies often right-hand side must occur left-hand side occurs, maxlen limits total number items rule. large data sets, setting support low maxlen high can produce extremely large rule set exhaust available memory. Start restrictive values relax needed. Rules often sorted interest measure inspection. Lift common choice. Use ordinary subsetting expressions focus particular consequent minimum quality value.
code: rules <- apriori(   trans,   parameter = list(support = 0.25, confidence = 0.6, maxlen = 5),   control = list(verbose = FALSE) ) rules #> set of 10 rules inspect(sort(rules, by = "lift")) #>      lhs               rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1]  {beer}         => {chips}  0.250   1.0000000  0.250    4.000000 2     #> [2]  {chips}        => {beer}   0.250   1.0000000  0.250    4.000000 2     #> [3]  {jam}          => {bread}  0.250   1.0000000  0.250    1.333333 2     #> [4]  {milk}         => {butter} 0.250   0.6666667  0.375    1.333333 2     #> [5]  {milk}         => {bread}  0.375   1.0000000  0.375    1.333333 3     #> [6]  {butter}       => {bread}  0.500   1.0000000  0.500    1.333333 4     #> [7]  {bread}        => {butter} 0.500   0.6666667  0.750    1.333333 4     #> [8]  {butter, milk} => {bread}  0.250   1.0000000  0.250    1.333333 2     #> [9]  {bread, milk}  => {butter} 0.250   0.6666667  0.375    1.333333 2     #> [10] {}             => {bread}  0.750   0.7500000  1.000    1.000000 6 butter_rules <- subset(rules, rhs %in% "butter" & lift > 1) inspect(butter_rules) #>     lhs              rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1] {milk}        => {butter} 0.25    0.6666667  0.375    1.333333 2     #> [2] {bread}       => {butter} 0.50    0.6666667  0.750    1.333333 4     #> [3] {bread, milk} => {butter} 0.25    0.6666667  0.375    1.333333 2

title: Interest measures
text: interestMeasure() calculates additional measures. Supply transactions measures require counts stored rules. , leverage observed joint support minus support expected independence. Phi correlation left- right-hand sides rule; undefined rules. Add selected measures new columns quality data frame. new measures can now used filter sort rules.
code: measures <- interestMeasure(   rules,   measure = c("leverage", "phi"),   transactions = trans ) head(measures) #>   leverage        phi #> 1  0.00000        NaN #> 2  0.00000        NaN #> 3  0.00000        NaN #> 4 -0.03125 -0.1490712 #> 5  0.06250  0.2581989 #> 6  0.06250  0.2581989 quality(rules) <- cbind(   quality(rules),   interestMeasure(     rules,     measure = c("leverage", "phi"),     transactions = trans   ) ) inspect(head(sort(rules, by = "leverage"), 3)) #>     lhs                rhs    support confidence coverage lift count leverage #> [1] {cookies, milk} => {tea}  0.250   1.00       0.250    1.6  2     0.09375  #> [2] {milk}          => {tea}  0.375   0.75       0.500    1.2  3     0.06250  #> [3] {tea}           => {milk} 0.375   0.60       0.625    1.2  3     0.06250  #>     phi       #> [1] 0.4472136 #> [2] 0.2581989 #> [3] 0.2581989

title: Item hierarchies
text: aggregate() replaces item labels group. Multiple items group one basket become single group item. Mine aggregated transactions analysis intended operate group level. calculates valid quality measures level.
code: by_category <- aggregate(trans, by = "category") inspect(trans) #>     items                   transactionID #> [1] {apple, banana}         T1            #> [2] {apple, yogurt}         T2            #> [3] {banana, milk}          T3            #> [4] {apple, banana, milk}   T4            #> [5] {milk, yogurt}          T5            #> [6] {apple, banana, yogurt} T6 inspect(by_category) #>     items          transactionID #> [1] {fruit}        T1            #> [2] {dairy, fruit} T2            #> [3] {dairy, fruit} T3            #> [4] {dairy, fruit} T4            #> [5] {dairy}        T5            #> [6] {dairy, fruit} T6 itemFrequency(by_category) #>     dairy     fruit  #> 0.8333333 0.8333333 category_rules <- apriori(   by_category,   parameter = list(support = 0.3, confidence = 0.5, minlen = 2),   control = list(verbose = FALSE) ) inspect(category_rules) #>     lhs        rhs     support   confidence coverage  lift count #> [1] {fruit} => {dairy} 0.6666667 0.8        0.8333333 0.96 4     #> [2] {dairy} => {fruit} 0.6666667 0.8        0.8333333 0.96 4

title: Item hierarchies
text: addAggregate() retains items adds group items. default, group items marked asterisk. creates rules cross levels. Adding category items creates trivial rules {apple} => {fruit*} hierarchy guarantees . filterAggregate() removes associations contain detailed item aggregate. reduces size rule set significantly makes easier interpret.
code: multilevel <- addAggregate(trans, by = "category") inspect(multilevel) #>     items                                   transactionID #> [1] {apple, banana, fruit*}                 T1            #> [2] {apple, yogurt, dairy*, fruit*}         T2            #> [3] {banana, milk, dairy*, fruit*}          T3            #> [4] {apple, banana, milk, dairy*, fruit*}   T4            #> [5] {milk, yogurt, dairy*}                  T5            #> [6] {apple, banana, yogurt, dairy*, fruit*} T6  multilevel_rules <- apriori(   multilevel,   parameter = list(support = 0.1, confidence = 0.6, minlen = 2),   control = list(verbose = FALSE) ) multilevel_rules #> set of 83 rules multilevel_rules <- filterAggregate(multilevel_rules) multilevel_rules #> set of 17 rules title: Mining and pruning association rules
text: Support, confidence, rule length constrain rule set Apriori searching. appearance argument can also restrict items left- right-hand side. , Apriori generates rules predict butter milk. constraints produce 4 rules. Constraining search also reduces memory computation requirements.
code: rules <- apriori(   trans,   parameter = list(     support = 0.25, confidence = 0.6,     maxlen = 3   ),   appearance = list(     rhs = c("butter", "milk"),     default = "lhs"   ) ) #> Apriori #>  #> Parameter specification: #>  confidence minval smax arem  aval originalSupport maxtime support minlen #>         0.6    0.1    1 none FALSE            TRUE       5    0.25      1 #>  maxlen target  ext #>       3  rules TRUE #>  #> Algorithmic control: #>  filter tree heap memopt load sort verbose #>     0.1 TRUE TRUE  FALSE TRUE    2    TRUE #>  #> Absolute minimum support count: 2  #>  #> set item appearances ...[2 item(s)] done [0.00s]. #> set transactions ...[5 item(s), 8 transaction(s)] done [0.00s]. #> sorting and recoding items ... [4 item(s)] done [0.00s]. #> creating transaction tree ... done [0.00s]. #> checking subsets of size 1 2 3 done [0.00s]. #> writing ... [4 rule(s)] done [0.00s]. #> creating S4 object  ... done [0.00s]. inspect(rules) #>     lhs             rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1] {}           => {butter} 0.750   0.7500000  1.000    1.000000 6     #> [2] {jam}        => {butter} 0.375   1.0000000  0.375    1.333333 3     #> [3] {bread}      => {butter} 0.625   0.7142857  0.875    0.952381 5     #> [4] {bread, jam} => {butter} 0.250   1.0000000  0.250    1.333333 2

title: Mining and pruning association rules
text: Filter criteria appropriate task, rank remaining rules. Keeping criteria code makes selection reproducible. Many interest measures available addition support, confidence, lift. vignette Interest measures (vignette("interest-measures", package = "arules")) introduces use additional interest measures.
code: selected <- subset(rules, lift > 1 & confidence >= 0.7) ranked <- sort(selected, by = "lift", decreasing = TRUE) inspect(ranked) #>     lhs             rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1] {jam}        => {butter} 0.375   1          0.375    1.333333 3     #> [2] {bread, jam} => {butter} 0.250   1          0.250    1.333333 2

title: Mining and pruning association rules
text: rule redundant general rule consequent performs least well according selected measure. Removing redundant rules produces concise result. complementary subset contains redundant rules removed.
code: non_redundant <- rules[!is.redundant(rules)] inspect(sort(non_redundant, by = "lift")) #>     lhs      rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1] {jam} => {butter} 0.375   1.00       0.375    1.333333 3     #> [2] {}    => {butter} 0.750   0.75       1.000    1.000000 6 inspect(rules[is.redundant(rules)]) #>     lhs             rhs      support confidence coverage lift     count #> [1] {bread}      => {butter} 0.625   0.7142857  0.875    0.952381 5     #> [2] {bread, jam} => {butter} 0.250   1.0000000  0.250    1.333333 2

title: Preparing transaction data
text: Use one character vector per transaction. List names become transaction IDs. Check transaction summary resulting item labels. item labels confirm baskets translated correctly.
code: baskets <- list(   order_1 = c("apple", "bread"),   order_2 = c("bread", "milk"),   order_3 = c("apple", "bread", "milk") ) from_list <- transactions(baskets) inspect(from_list) #>     items                transactionID #> [1] {apple, bread}       order_1       #> [2] {bread, milk}        order_2       #> [3] {apple, bread, milk} order_3 summary(from_list) #> transactions as itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  3 rows (elements/itemsets/transactions) and #>  3 columns (items) and a density of 0.7777778  #>  #> most frequent items: #>   bread   apple    milk (Other)  #>       3       2       2       0  #>  #> element (itemset/transaction) length distribution: #> sizes #> 2 3  #> 2 1  #>  #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  #>   2.000   2.000   2.000   2.333   2.500   3.000  #>  #> includes extended item information - examples: #>   labels #> 1  apple #> 2  bread #> 3   milk #>  #> includes extended transaction information - examples: #>   transactionID #> 1       order_1 #> 2       order_2 #> 3       order_3 itemLabels(from_list) #> [1] "apple" "bread" "milk"

title: Preparing transaction data
text: Rows represent transactions columns represent items. Logical matrices make intended coding explicit.
code: binary <- matrix(   c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE,     FALSE, TRUE, TRUE,     TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),   nrow = 3,   byrow = TRUE,   dimnames = list(names(baskets), c("apple", "bread", "milk")) ) from_matrix <- transactions(binary)  itemLabels(from_matrix) #> [1] "apple" "bread" "milk" inspect(from_matrix) #>     items                transactionID #> [1] {apple, bread}       order_1       #> [2] {bread, milk}        order_2       #> [3] {apple, bread, milk} order_3

what: A data frame in wide format
title: Preparing transaction data
text: Categorical columns converted items form variable=value. Logical columns represent presence absence single item. Missing values omitted. Continuous variables need discretized conversion.
code: customers <- data.frame(   age_group = factor(c("young", "adult", "adult")),   region = factor(c("north", "south", "north")),   subscriber = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) ) from_wide <- transactions(customers)  itemLabels(from_wide) #> [1] "age_group=adult" "age_group=young" "region=north"    "region=south"    #> [5] "subscriber" inspect(from_wide) #>     items                                       transactionID #> [1] {age_group=young, region=north, subscriber} 1             #> [2] {age_group=adult, region=south}             2             #> [3] {age_group=adult, region=north, subscriber} 3 measurements <- data.frame(   spend = c(12, 18, 35, 42, 55),   visits = c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8) ) measurements_discrete <- discretizeDF(   measurements,   default = list(method = "frequency", breaks = 2) ) from_discrete <- transactions(measurements_discrete)  itemLabels(from_discrete) #> [1] "spend=[12,35)" "spend=[35,55]" "visits=[1,3)"  "visits=[3,8]" inspect(from_discrete) #>     items                         transactionID #> [1] {spend=[12,35), visits=[1,3)} 1             #> [2] {spend=[12,35), visits=[1,3)} 2             #> [3] {spend=[35,55], visits=[3,8]} 3             #> [4] {spend=[35,55], visits=[3,8]} 4             #> [5] {spend=[35,55], visits=[3,8]} 5

what: A data frame in long format
title: Preparing transaction data
text: Long-format data one row per transaction–item pair. Identify transaction item columns cols.
code: long <- data.frame(   order = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3),   product = c("apple", "bread", "bread", "milk", "apple") ) from_long <- transactions(long, format = "long", cols = c("order", "product"))  itemLabels(from_long) #> [1] "apple" "bread" "milk" inspect(from_long) #>     items          transactionID #> [1] {apple, bread} 1             #> [2] {bread, milk}  2             #> [3] {apple}        3

title: Mining Association Rules and Frequent Itemsets
text: arules: arules base package data structures, mining algorithms (APRIORI ECLAT), interest measures. arulesViz: Visualization association rules. arulesCBA: Classification algorithms based association rules (includes CBA). arulesSequences: Mining frequent sequences (cSPADE).

title: Mining Association Rules and Frequent Itemsets
text: Additional mining algorithms arulesNBMiner: Mining NB-frequent itemsets NB-precise rules. fim4r: Provides fast implementations several mining algorithms. interface function called fim4r() provided arules. opusminer: OPUS Miner algorithm finding top-k productive, non-redundant itemsets. Call opus() format = 'itemsets'. -database analytics ibmdbR: IBM -database analytics R can calculate association rules database table. Interface rattle: Provides graphical user interface association rule mining. pmml: Generates PMML (predictive model markup language) association rules. Classification arc: Alternative CBA implementation. rCBA: Alternative CBA implementation. qCBA: Quantitative Classification Association Rules. sblr: Scalable Bayesian rule lists algorithm classification. Recommendation/Prediction recommenderlab: Supports creating predictions using association rules. following R packages use arules: arc, arlclustering, arulesCBA, arulesNBMiner, arulesSequences, arulesViz, clickstream, CLONETv2, CRE, ctsem, daltoolbox, discnorm, fcaR, fdm2id, gp3sequences, GroupBN, ibmdbR, icdhelper, manydist, nuggets, opusminer, pervasive, pmml, qCBA, RareComb, rattle, rCBA, recommenderlab, rgnoisefilt, RulesTools, sbrl, SurvivalTests, TELP, tidylearn

title: Mining Associations with the Apriori Algorithm — apriori
text: Apriori algorithm (Agrawal et al, 1993) employs level-wise search frequent itemsets. used C implementation Apriori Christian Borgelt (2003) includes improvements (e.g., prefix tree item sorting). Warning automatic conversion matrices data.frames transactions. preferred create transactions manually calling apriori() control item coding. especially important working multiple datasets several subsets dataset. read item coding, see itemCoding. data.frame specified x, data automatically converted transactions discretizing numeric data using discretizeDF() coercion transactions. discretization may fail data well behaved. Apriori creates rules one item RHS (Consequent). default value APparameter minlen 1. meains rules one item (.e., empty antecedent/LHS) like $$\{\} => \{beer\}$$ created.  rules mean matter items involved, item RHS appear probability given rule's confidence (equals support).  want avoid rules use argument parameter = list(minlen = 2). Notes run time memory usage: minimum support chosen low dataset, algorithm try create extremely large set itemsets/rules. result long run time eventually process run memory.  prevent , default maximal length itemsets/rules restricted 10 items (via parameter element maxlen = 10) time checking subsets limited 5 seconds (via maxtime = 5). output show hit limits "checking subsets" line output. time limit checked subset size increases, may run significantly longer specify maxtime.  Setting maxtime = 0 disables time limit. Interrupting execution Control-C/Esc recommended.  Memory cleanup prevented resulting memory leak. We first mine all rules. inspect(fim4r(Adult,   method = "fpgrowth",   target = "rules", support = .8 ))  # ignore item "capital-gain=None" inspect(fim4r(Adult,   method = "fpgrowth",   target = "rules", support = .8,   appear = list(c("capital-gain=None"), c("-")) ))  # "capital-gain=None" cannot appear in consequent (antecedent only) inspect(fim4r(Adult,   method = "fpgrowth",   target = "rules", support = .8,   appear = list(c("capital-gain=None"), c("a")) ))  # "capital-gain=None" cannot appear in the antecedent inspect(fim4r(Adult,   method = "fpgrowth",   target = "rules", support = .8,   appear = list(c("capital-gain=None"), c("c")) ))  # restrict the consequent to the item "capital-gain=None". # That is, "" = all items can only appear in the antecedent with the # exception that "capital-gain=None" can only appear in the consequent. inspect(fim4r(Adult,   method = "fpgrowth",   target = "rules", support = .8,   appear = list(c("", "capital-gain=None"), c("a", "c")) )) } # }

title: Calculate Additional Interest Measures — interestMeasure
text: x set itemsets rules. measure name vector names desired interest measures (see Details section available measures). measure missing available measures calculated. transactions transactions used mine associations set different transactions calculate interest measures (Note: need set reuse = FALSE later case). reuse logical indicating information quality slot reuse calculating measures. speeds process significantly since little () transaction counting necessary support, confidence lift already available. Use reuse = FALSE force counting (might slow necessary use different set transactions used mining). ... arguments measure calculation. Many measures based contingency table counts zero counts can produce NaN values (division zero). issue can resolved using additional parameter smoothCounts performs additive smoothing adds "pseudo count" smoothCounts cell contingency table. Use smoothCounts = 1 larger values Laplace smoothing. Use smoothCounts = .5 Haldane-Anscombe correction (Haldan, 1940; Anscombe, 1956) often used chi-squared, phi correlation related measures.

title: Calculate Additional Interest Measures — interestMeasure
text: searchable list definitions, equations references available interest measures can found https://mhahsler.github.io/arules/docs/measures. descriptions also linked list . following measures implemented itemsets: "support": Support. "count": Support Count. "allConfidence": -Confidence. "crossSupportRatio": Cross-Support Ratio. "lift": Lift. following measures implemented rules: "support": Support. "confidence": Confidence. "lift": Lift. "count": Support Count. "addedValue": Added Value. "boost": Confidence Boost. "causalConfidence": Causal Confidence. "causalSupport": Causal Support. "accuracy": Accuracy. "balancedAccuracy": Balanced Accuracy. "centeredConfidence": Centered Confidence. "certainty": Certainty Factor. "chiSquared": Chi-Squared. Additional parameters : significance = TRUE returns p-value test independence instead chi-squared statistic. p-values, substitution effects (occurrence one item makes occurrence another item less likely) can tested using parameter complements = FALSE.  Note: Correction multiple comparisons can done using stats::p.adjust(). "collectiveStrength": Collective Strength. "confirmedConfidence": Descriptive Confirmed Confidence. "conviction": Conviction. "cosine": Cosine. "counterexample": Example Counter-Example Rate. "coverage": Coverage. "doc": Difference Confidence. "fishersExactTest": Fisher's Exact Test. default complementary effects mined, substitutes can found using parameter complements = FALSE. Note Fisher's exact test equal hyper-confidence significance = TRUE. Correction multiple comparisons can done using stats::p.adjust(). "gini": Gini Index. "hyperConfidence": Hyper-Confidence. Reports confidence level default significance level significance = TRUE used. default complementary effects mined, substitutes (low co-occurrence counts) can found using parameter complements = FALSE. "hyperLift": Hyper-Lift. used quantile can changed using parameter level (default: level = 0.99). "imbalance": Imbalance Ratio. "implicationIndex": Implication Index. "importance": Importance. "improvement": Improvement. additional parameter improvementMeasure (default: 'confidence') can used specify measure used improvement calculation. See Generalized improvement. "jaccard": Jaccard Coefficient. "jMeasure": J-Measure. "kappa": Kappa. "kulczynski": Kulczynski. "lambda": Lambda. "laplace": Laplace Corrected Confidence. Parameter k can used specify number classes (default 2). "leastContradiction": Least Contradiction. "lerman": Lerman Similarity. "leverage": Leverage. "LIC": Lift Increase. additional parameter improvementMeasure (default: 'lift') can used specify measure used increase calculation.  See Generalized increase ratio. "maxconfidence": Max-Confidence. "mutualInformation": Mutual Information. "netconf": Netconf. "oddsRatio": Odds Ratio. "phi": Phi Correlation Coefficient. "ralambondrainy": Ralambondrainy. "relativeRisk": Relative Risk. "rhsSupport": Right-Hand-Side Support. "RLD": Relative Linkage Disequilibrium. "rulePowerFactor": Rule Power Factor. "precision": Precision. "recall": Recall. "fScore": F-score. "sebag": Sebag-Schoenauer. "stdLift": Standardized Lift. "table": Contingency Table. Returns four counts contingency table. entries labeled n11, n01, n10, n00 (first subscript X second Y; 1 indicated presence 0 indicates absence). several measures specified, counts prefix table. "varyingLiaison": Varying Rates Liaison. "zhang": Zhang's Measure. "yuleQ": Yule's Q. "yuleY": Yule's Y.

itemLabels = Adult) image(sub.recoded)    ## Example 4: manually create 2 new transaction for the Adult data set ##            Note: check itemLabels(Adult) to see the available labels for items twoTransactions <- as(   encode(list(     c("age=Young", "relationship=Unmarried"),     c("age=Senior")   ), itemLabels = Adult),   "transactions" )  twoTransactions #> transactions in sparse format [1] {age=Young, relationship=Unmarried} #> [2] {age=Senior}                         ## Example 5: Use a common item coding  # Creation of transactions separately will produce different item codings (rows) and #>  4 items (columns)  compatible(trans1, trans2) #> [1] FALSE  # produce common item coding (all item labels in the two sets) commonItemLabels <- union(itemLabels(trans1), itemLabels(trans2)) commonItemLabels #> [1] "age=Senior"             "age=Young"              "relationship=Unmarried" #> [4] "age=Middle-aged"        "relationship=Married"    trans1 <- recode(trans1, itemLabels = commonItemLabels) trans1 #> transactions in sparse format with #>  2 transactions (rows) and #>  5 items (columns) trans2 <- recode(trans2, itemLabels = commonItemLabels) trans2 #> transactions in sparse format with #>  2 transactions (rows) and #>  5 items (columns)  compatible(trans1, trans2) #> [1] TRUE   ## Example 6: manually create a rule using the item coding in Adult ## and calculate interest measures aRule <- new("rules",   lhs = encode(list(c("age=Young", "relationship=Unmarried")),     itemLabels = Adult   ),   rhs = encode(list(c("income=small")),     itemLabels = Adult   ) )  ## shorter version using the rules constructor aRule <- rules(   lhs = list(c("age=Young", "relationship=Unmarried")),   rhs = list(c("income=small")),   itemLabels = Adult )  quality(aRule) <- interestMeasure(aRule,   measure = c("support", "confidence", "lift"), transactions = Adult )  inspect(aRule) #>     lhs                                    rhs            support title: Class itemMatrix — Sparse Binary Incidence Matrix to Represent Sets of Items — itemMatrix-class
text: Representation Sets itemsets represented compressed sparse binary matrix. Conceptually, columns represent items rows sets/transactions. compressed form, itemset vector column indices (called item IDs) representing items. Warning: Ideally, store matrix row-oriented sparse matrix (ngRMatrix), Matrix package provides better support column-oriented sparse classes (Matrix::ngCMatrix). matrix therefore internally stored transposed form. Working several itemMatrix objects work several itemMatrix objects time (e.g., several transaction sets, lhs rhs rule, etc.), encoding (itemLabes order items binary matrix) different itemMatrices important needs conform. See itemCoding learn encode recode itemMatrix objects.

code: set.seed(1234)  ## Generate a logical matrix with 5000 random itemsets for 20 items m <- matrix(runif(5000 * 20) > 0.8,   ncol = 20,   dimnames = list(NULL, paste("item", c(1:20), sep = "")) ) head(m) #>      item1 item2 item3 item4 item5 item6 item7 item8 item9 item10 item11 item12 #> [1,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE #> [2,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [3,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [4,] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [5,]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [6,] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #>      item13 item14 item15 item16 item17 item18 item19 item20 #> [1,]   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE #> [2,]  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [3,]  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [4,]  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> [5,]  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE #> [6,]  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  ## Coerce the logical matrix into an itemMatrix object imatrix <- as(m, "itemMatrix") imatrix #> itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  5000 rows (elements/transactions) and #>  20 columns (items)  ## An itemMatrix contains a set of itemsets (each row is an itemset). ## The length of the set is the number of rows. length(imatrix) #> [1] 5000  ## The sparese matrix also has regular matrix  dimensions. dim(imatrix) #> [1] 5000   20 nrow(imatrix) #> [1] 5000 ncol(imatrix) #> [1] 20  ## Subsetting: Get first 5 elements (rows) of the itemMatrix. This can be done in ## several ways. imatrix[1:5] ### get elements 1:5 #> itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  5 rows (elements/transactions) and #>  20 columns (items) imatrix[1:5, ] ### Matrix subsetting for rows 1:5 #> itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  5 rows (elements/transactions) and #>  20 columns (items) head(imatrix, n = 5) ### head() #> itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  5 rows (elements/transactions) and #>  20 columns (items)  ## Get first 5 elements (rows) of the itemMatrix as list. as(imatrix[1:5], "list") #> $`1` #> [1] "item7"  "item10" "item13" "item15" "item18" "item20" #>  #> $`2` #> [1] "item5"  "item7"  "item17" #>  #> $`3` #> [1] "item15" #>  #> $`4` #> [1] "item3" "item8" #>  #> $`5` #> [1] "item1"  "item8"  "item20" #>   ## Get first 5 elements (rows) of the itemMatrix as matrix. as(imatrix[1:5], "matrix") #>   item1 item2 item3 item4 item5 item6 item7 item8 item9 item10 item11 item12 #> 1 FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE #> 2 FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 3 FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 4 FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 5  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #>   item13 item14 item15 item16 item17 item18 item19 item20 #> 1   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE   TRUE #> 2  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 3  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 4  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE #> 5  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE   TRUE  ## Get first 5 elements (rows) of the itemMatrix as sparse ngCMatrix. ## **Warning:** For efficiency reasons, the ngCMatrix is transposed! You ## can transpose it again to get the expected format. as(imatrix[1:5], "ngCMatrix") #> 20 x 5 sparse Matrix of class "ngCMatrix" #>        1 2 3 4 5 #> item1  . . . . | #> item2  . . . . . #> item3  . . . | . #> item4  . . . . . #> item5  . | . . . #> item6  . . . . . #> item7  | | . . . #> item8  . . . | | #> item9  . . . . . #> item10 | . . . . #> item11 . . . . . #> item12 . . . . . #> item13 | . . . . #> item14 . . . . . #> item15 | . | . . #> item16 . . . . . #> item17 . | . . . #> item18 | . . . . #> item19 . . . . . #> item20 | . . . | t(as(imatrix[1:5], "ngCMatrix")) #> 5 x 20 sparse Matrix of class "ngCMatrix" #>   [[ suppressing 20 column names ‘item1’, ‘item2’, ‘item3’ ... ]] #>                                           #> 1 . . . . . . | . . | . . | . | . . | . | #> 2 . . . . | . | . . . . . . . . . | . . . #> 3 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . | . . . . . #> 4 . . | . . . . | . . . . . . . . . . . . #> 5 | . . . . . . | . . . . . . . . . . . |  ## Get labels for the first 5 itemsets (first default and then with ## custom formating) labels(imatrix[1:5]) #> [1] "{item7,item10,item13,item15,item18,item20}" #> [2] "{item5,item7,item17}"                       #> [3] "{item15}"                                   #> [4] "{item3,item8}"                              #> [5] "{item1,item8,item20}"                       labels(imatrix[1:5], itemSep = " + ", setStart = "", setEnd = "") #> [1] "item7 + item10 + item13 + item15 + item18 + item20" #> [2] "item5 + item7 + item17"                             #> [3] "item15"                                             #> [4] "item3 + item8"                                      #> [5] "item1 + item8 + item20"                              ## Create itemsets manually from an itemMatrix. Itemsets contain items in the form of ## an itemMatrix and additional quality measures (not supplied in the example). is <- new("itemsets", items = imatrix) is #> set of 5000 itemsets  inspect(head(is, n = 3)) #>     items                                           #> [1] {item7, item10, item13, item15, item18, item20} #> [2] {item5, item7, item17}                          #> [3] {item15}                                          ## Create rules manually. I use imatrix[4:6] for the lhs of the rules and ## imatrix[1:3] for the rhs. Rhs and lhs cannot share items so I use ## itemSetdiff here. I also assign missing values for the quality measures support ## and confidence. rules <- new("rules",   lhs = itemSetdiff(imatrix[4:6], imatrix[1:3]),   rhs = imatrix[1:3],   quality = data.frame(     support = c(NA, NA, NA),     confidence = c(NA, NA, NA)   ) ) rules #> set of 3 rules  inspect(rules) #>     lhs          rhs       support confidence #> [1] {item3,                                   #>      item8}   => {item7,                      #>                   item10,                     #>                   item13,                     #>                   item15,                     #>                   item18,                     #>                   item20}       NA         NA #> [2] {item1,                                   #>      item8,                                   #>      item20}  => {item5,                      #>                   item7,                      #>                   item17}       NA         NA #> [3] {item9,                                   #>      item17,                                  #>      item18}  => {item15}       NA         NA  ## Manually create a itemMatrix with an item encoding that matches imatrix (20 items in order ## item1, item2, ..., item20) itemset_list <- list(   c("item1", "item2"),   c("item3") )  imatrix_new <- encode(itemset_list, itemLabels = imatrix) imatrix_new #> itemMatrix in sparse format with #>  2 rows (elements/transactions) and #>  20 columns (items) compatible(imatrix_new, imatrix) #> [1] TRUE

"agrawal" (see Agrawal Srikant, 1994): method creates transactions correlated items using random.patters(). simulation two-stage process. First, set nPats patterns (potential maximal frequent itemsets) generated.  length patterns Poisson distributed mean lPats consecutive patterns share items controlled correlation parameter corr.  later use, pattern pattern weight generated drawing exponential distribution mean 1 corruption level chosen normal distribution mean cmean variance cvar. function returns patterns itemsets objects can supplied random.transactions() argument patterns.  argument patterns supplied, default values given used. second step, transactions generated using patterns.  length transactions follows Poisson distribution mean lPats. transaction, patterns randomly chosen using pattern weights till transaction length reached. chosen pattern, associated corruption level used drop items adding pattern transaction.

title: Association Rule Induction from Itemsets — ruleInduction
text: rules can created using supplied itemsets surpass specified minimum confidence threshold returned. ruleInduction() can used produce closed association rules defined Pei et al. (2000) rules X => Y X Y closed frequent itemsets. See code example Example section. Rule induction implements two methods. default "ptree". "ptree" method without transactions: transactions need specified x contains complete set frequent itemsets. itemsets' support counts stored ptree retrieved create rules calculate confidence. fast, fails support values missing x complete set frequent itemsets. "ptree" method transactions: transactions specified transactions counted prefix tree later retrieved create rules itemsets calculate confidence values. slower, necessary x complete set frequent itemsets. improve speed, unused items removed transaction data creating prefix tree (behavior can changed using argument reduce). might slower large transaction data sets. However, highly recommended items also reordered reduce counting time. "apriori" method (always needs transactions): association rules mined transactions data set using apriori() smallest support found itemsets. second step, rules generated one itemsets removed. procedure slow, especially itemsets many elements low support.

title: Support Counting for Itemsets — support
text: Normally, support frequent itemsets counted efficiently mining process using minimum support threshold. However, support specific itemsets (maybe itemsets low support) needed, support set itemsets needs recalculated different transactions mined , support() can used. Several methods support counting available: "ptree" (default method): counters itemsets organized prefix tree. transactions sequentially processed corresponding counters prefix tree incremented (see Hahsler et al, 2008). method used default since typically significantly faster transaction ID list intersection. "tidlists": Support counted using transaction ID list intersection used several fast mining algorithms (e.g., Eclat). However, support determined itemset individually slow large number long itemsets dense data. item coding x transactions reconciled using item labels. Items occur transactions affect count. reduce = TRUE, unused items removed prefix-tree counting. Weighted support uses numeric weight column transactionInfo(transactions). Absolute weighted support sum weights supporting transactions; relative weighted support divides value sum transaction weights.

code: ## Example 1: SunBai data data(SunBai) SunBai #> transactions in sparse format with #>  6 transactions (rows) and #>  8 items (columns)  ## weights are stored in transactionInfo transactionInfo(SunBai) #>   transactionID    weight #> 1           100 0.5176528 #> 2           200 0.4362571 #> 3           300 0.2321374 #> 4           400 0.1476262 #> 5           500 0.5440458 #> 6           600 0.4123691  ## mine weighted support itemsets using transaction support in SunBai s <- weclat(SunBai,   parameter = list(support = 0.3),   control = list(verbose = TRUE) ) #> Weighted Eclat (WEclat) #>  #> parameter specification: #>  support minlen maxlen target ext #>      0.3      1     10   <NA>  NA #>  #> algorithmic control: #>  sort verbose #>    NA    TRUE #>  #> preparing ... 8 items, 6 L1 [0.00s] #> mining ... 6 transactions, 0.33 used [0.00s] #> writing ... 12 itemsets [0.00s] inspect(sort(s)) #>      items     support   #> [1]  {C}       0.6541039 #> [2]  {G}       0.6081302 #> [3]  {A}       0.5719366 #> [4]  {F}       0.4280634 #> [5]  {F, G}    0.4280634 #> [6]  {C, F, G} 0.4280634 #> [7]  {C, F}    0.4280634 #> [8]  {C, G}    0.4280634 #> [9]  {H}       0.4176323 #> [10] {G, H}    0.4176323 #> [11] {B}       0.3274066 #> [12] {A, B}    0.3274066  ## create rules using weighted support (satisfying a minimum ## weighted confidence of 90%). r <- ruleInduction(s, confidence = .9) inspect(r) #>     lhs       rhs support   confidence lift     #> [1] {B}    => {A} 0.3274066 1          1.748445 #> [2] {H}    => {G} 0.4176323 1          1.644385 #> [3] {F}    => {G} 0.4280634 1          1.644385 #> [4] {F, G} => {C} 0.4280634 1          1.528809 #> [5] {C, G} => {F} 0.4280634 1          2.336103 #> [6] {C, F} => {G} 0.4280634 1          1.644385 #> [7] {F}    => {C} 0.4280634 1          1.528809  ## Example 2: Find association rules in weighted data trans <- list(   c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),   c("C", "F", "G"),   c("A", "B"),   c("A"),   c("C", "F", "G", "H"),   c("A", "G", "H") )  weight <- c(5, 10, 6, 7, 5, 1)  ## convert list to transactions trans <- transactions(trans)  ## add weight information transactionInfo(trans) <- data.frame(weight = weight) inspect(trans) #>     items           weight #> [1] {A, B, C, D, E}  5     #> [2] {C, F, G}       10     #> [3] {A, B}           6     #> [4] {A}              7     #> [5] {C, F, G, H}     5     #> [6] {A, G, H}        1      ## mine weighed support itemsets s <- weclat(trans,   parameter = list(support = 0.3),   control = list(verbose = TRUE) ) #> Weighted Eclat (WEclat) #>  #> parameter specification: #>  support minlen maxlen target ext #>      0.3      1     10   <NA>  NA #>  #> algorithmic control: #>  sort verbose #>    NA    TRUE #>  #> preparing ... 8 items, 5 L1 [0.00s] #> mining ... 6 transactions, 0.28 used [0.00s] #> writing ... 10 itemsets [0.00s] inspect(sort(s)) #>      items     support   #> [1]  {C}       0.5882353 #> [2]  {A}       0.5588235 #> [3]  {G}       0.4705882 #> [4]  {F}       0.4411765 #> [5]  {F, G}    0.4411765 #> [6]  {C, F, G} 0.4411765 #> [7]  {C, F}    0.4411765 #> [8]  {C, G}    0.4411765 #> [9]  {B}       0.3235294 #> [10] {A, B}    0.3235294  ## create association rules r <- ruleInduction(s, confidence = .5) inspect(r) #>      lhs       rhs support   confidence lift     #> [1]  {B}    => {A} 0.3235294 1.0000000  1.789474 #> [2]  {A}    => {B} 0.3235294 0.5789474  1.789474 #> [3]  {G}    => {F} 0.4411765 0.9375000  2.125000 #> [4]  {F}    => {G} 0.4411765 1.0000000  2.125000 #> [5]  {F, G} => {C} 0.4411765 1.0000000  1.700000 #> [6]  {C, G} => {F} 0.4411765 1.0000000  2.266667 #> [7]  {C, F} => {G} 0.4411765 1.0000000  2.125000 #> [8]  {F}    => {C} 0.4411765 1.0000000  1.700000 #> [9]  {C}    => {F} 0.4411765 0.7500000  1.700000 #> [10] {G}    => {C} 0.4411765 0.9375000  1.593750 #> [11] {C}    => {G} 0.4411765 0.7500000  1.593750
